# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>
response:
# Critical Reading: Evidence Briefing, Synthesis of Five Sources

This briefing is accurate on most points and well calibrated overall. Its central conclusions match my reading of the five sources:

- The per-hour gain is real but modest.
- The figures above 20% come from weak measurement.
- Output per worker falls slightly in discretionary work.
- Coverage-bound work loses output and service.
- Whether the gain requires the hours cut is the key open question.

But it has one factual error, a table whose ordering overstates a trend, a per-worker range that is slightly optimistic, and several caveats lost in condensing. For a policy audience, the biggest gap is cost, which it never addresses.

Some caveats below come from the source documents themselves. Others come from my earlier readings, such as the queueing interpretation and the ambiguity in the system logs. I note which is which, because the briefing can fairly be held to the first but only advised on the second.

## What it does well

- **It traces how later sources qualify earlier ones.** It doesn't simply average them.
- **It separates source 3's well-supported corrections from its unsupported conclusion,** and makes the same separation for source 4.
- **It keeps per-hour and per-worker productivity distinct throughout.** This is the most important conceptual point in the whole body of evidence.
- **It states that sickness and turnover benefits are not productivity,** and that their offsetting value is not estimated.
- **Its open questions are the right ones,** especially whether reorganising work alone could deliver the gain without the hours cut.
- **It rejects both slogans:** "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage".

## Factual and arithmetic check

Most figures are transcribed correctly. These are not:

**1. The source 5 decline compares two different measures.** The briefing says "the per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours)". But 12.5% is the 9-month timesheet figure, and 8.5% is the 24-month log figure. Part of that 4-point drop comes from switching measures, not from the passage of time. Source 5 makes the like-for-like comparison itself: **12.5% → 9.8% on timesheets**. The briefing therefore overstates the decline. It also omits source 5's caution that the decline is "consistent with some fading", with heavily overlapping intervals.

**2. The per-worker range is slightly optimistic.** Point 2 in section 3 says output per worker is "around 2 to 4% lower". Applying the briefing's own ranges:

| Hours change | Per-hour gain | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|
| −11% | +10% | 0.89 × 1.10 = 0.979 → −2.1% |
| −11% | +8.5% | 0.89 × 1.085 = 0.966 → −3.4% |
| −14% | +10% | 0.86 × 1.10 = 0.946 → −5.4% |
| −14% | +8% | 0.86 × 1.08 = 0.929 → −7.1% |

The direct estimates are −3.4% (Varden, 24 months), −2.7% (meta-analysis, controlled discretionary studies) and −4.1% (meta-analysis, all controlled studies). The derived figures run from about 2% to 7%. "Around 2 to 5%" would fit the direct estimates better, and the confidence intervals reach −8%.

**3. Source 4's duration claim was unsupported, not shown "wrong".** Source 5 showed the meta-analysis's long-follow-up evidence was unfit to test decay, and found a decline in point estimate in one controlled study. That decline is not statistically established. "Unsupported" is accurate. "Wrong" claims more than one trial with overlapping intervals can show.

**4. "Actual hours fell 14.1%" (source 3)** applies to the 27 organisations with time tracking, not the whole pilot. The briefing drops that qualifier.

## Issues

### 1. Table 1 is not in order of design strength, and the order affects the conclusion

The table says it is "ordered by strength of design" and concludes that "estimates fall as designs strengthen". The ordering doesn't support that:

- **The meta-analysis's all-studies figure (+13.4%) sits below two uncontrolled subsets**, yet it pools mostly weaker designs.
- **The 24-month Halden survivors (+11.8%) rank above the 6-month subset.** These are organisations that self-selected twice. Source 5 calls this an upper bound, not a stronger design.
- **The randomised 9-month estimate (+12.5%) is higher than the uncontrolled corrected subset (+10.8%)** and the bias-adjusted figure (+9.1%). So the decline is not monotonic.
- **The final row is counter work (+6.7%), a different type of work.** Putting it last makes the trend look steeper, but its lower value reflects the work type, not the design. As I argued in reading source 2, it probably reflects busier staff rather than better work.

The fair statement is narrower: **no design that measures actual hours finds more than about 12.5%.** In discretionary work, the stronger designs cluster around 8–12%. That still supports the briefing's conclusion without implying a clean ranking.

### 2. "Converge on 8 to 10%" repeats the meta-analysis's independence problem

The meta-analysis subgroups cited as converging (controlled, actual hours, record-based, controlled discretionary, bias-adjusted) largely contain the same studies, and the bias-adjusted figure relies on imputed studies. The briefing presents this as several independent confirmations. The more independent evidence is the agreement between source 5's randomised trial and source 3's corrected observational subset, since those use different designs. The briefing has that evidence available and could cite it instead.

### 3. "Same output in four days" is misleading even where it is nearly true

The briefing says "'Same output in four days' is close to true" in discretionary work. But the evidence shows actual hours fell only 11–14%, not 20%, because staff worked longer days, worked on the day off, or claimed overtime. Nearly the same output comes from roughly **4.3–4.5 days' worth of hours**, not four.

This matters for policy. Part of the "maintained output" comes from staff not actually taking the full reduction. Section 3, point 2 says so, but the slogan and the bottom line ("offsets the hours lost") blur it. A reader could take away that a 20% cut in time costs only about 3% of output. In fact, a roughly 12% cut in actual time costs about 3% of output.

### 4. The mediation finding loses its caveats

The briefing calls source 5's mediation analysis "a registered mediation test" and puts "about half... comes from removing recurring meetings" in its bottom line. Source 5 itself notes the analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding. My earlier reading added further concerns:

- The test was run on the same seven offices that generated the hypothesis. It shows the association persisted, not that it replicated.
- The effective sample is 14 offices, so the 28–66% interval is likely too narrow.
- Fatigue is measured less precisely than meeting time, so its 18% share is probably understated.
- It is unclear what the system logs measure. If they exclude meeting time, then output per log-hour is an awkward outcome for a meetings mediator.
- Two control offices cut their meetings partway through the trial, which contaminated the control arm.

The briefing also says source 3's meetings dismissal "does not survive later evidence". It is fairer to say it was partly answered: the model was pre-specified and tested on later data, but not on new offices.

For the bottom line, something like "in one trial, about half the per-hour gain was associated with fewer meetings" carries the right weight. Stating it as an established fact gives the finding more confidence than seven offices can support.

### 5. Cost is missing, and for a policy working group it is the main question

Every scheme in the evidence kept pay at full rates. So:

- **Discretionary work:** output per worker falls about 3%, so labour cost per unit of output rises by about 1/0.966 − 1 ≈ **3.5%**. Varden case-processing also paid overtime claimed to clear backlogs, which adds to this, and no source reports the overtime bill.
- **Coverage-bound work:** source 5 estimates about **+9%** cost per contact to restore service. That figure comes from one county, and it assumes labour is about three-quarters of total cost.
- **Offsets:** lower turnover cuts recruitment and training costs. None of the sources estimates those savings.

The open-questions list should include cost per unit of output and the net effect of turnover savings. A policy group will need both.

### 6. Sickness benefits may be partly double-counted

The briefing says the body doesn't estimate how far sickness and resignation benefits "offset per-worker output losses". But output per FTE is measured across all employees, including those off sick. So fewer sick days are **already counted** in the per-worker output figures. They are part of why the loss is only about 3%.

Adding sickness reduction on top as a separate offset would count it twice. Turnover savings are different: recruitment and training costs sit outside the output measures, so they are a genuine additional offset.

### 7. Coverage-bound conclusions rest on less than they appear to

- **"Maintaining service requires about 12% more staff"** is presented as general. It is a single estimate from one county's counter offices.
- **"Per-hour gains exist but are small"** is literally true, but in my earlier readings I argued the gain probably reflects fuller utilisation: fewer staff serving the same queue. Calling these "gains" invites readers to see them as efficiency.
- **The binary between the two types of work is leakier than the briefing suggests.** Source 5 reports that a Halden marketing agency reverted, citing client deadlines. That is nominally discretionary work. The meta-analysis also notes that most organisations mix both types of work. The briefing never mentions source 5's Halden reversions.

### 8. The evidence covers cuts of varying size, not exactly "a fifth"

The briefing frames its question as a 20% cut. The meta-analysis included cuts of at least 10%. Its implied average reduction in scheduled hours is about 15%, and in actual hours about 11–13%. Varden cut scheduled hours by 20%, from 37.5 to 30, but other studies cut less. The meta-analysis estimates are therefore not specific to a 20% cut. This is minor, but the scope statement should match the evidence.

### 9. Smaller omissions

- **Halden's 24-month follow-up had response bias:** 14 of 23 organisations replied, so 3 reversions is probably a minimum.
- **Some authors evaluated their own work.** In source 5, the Varden authors assessed their own hypothesis, and a Halden author followed up Halden's pilot. This is worth noting given how much weight the briefing puts on source 5.
- **The strongest evidence is from public administration.** The briefing lists this as an open question, which is good. It could go further: the 8–10% figure comes almost entirely from that sector.

## Suggested revisions

**Section 1, source 5:** "The per-hour gain declined from 12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets, and was 8.5% on the stricter log measure. The decline is consistent with some fading but is not statistically established."

**Section 3, point 2:** "Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 5% lower, with intervals that include zero. Near-maintained output partly reflects staff working more than the scheduled hours. Actual time fell about 12%, not 20%."

**Section 4, add:**
- Cost per unit of output, which no source reports, including the overtime bill and turnover savings.
- Whether the meetings mechanism replicates in new organisations.
- How mixed roles, and deadline-bound discretionary work, fare under the scheme.

**Bottom line:**
> A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay reduced actual hours by about 12%. In discretionary work, output per actual hour rose by roughly 8 to 10% after two years, down from about 12% in the first year. In the one trial that tested mechanisms, about half of the gain was associated with fewer meetings. Output per worker fell slightly, by about 2 to 5%, so labour cost per unit of output rose by a similar amount before any turnover savings. In coverage-bound work, output and service fell unless staff were added, at an estimated 9% higher cost per contact in one setting. Whether reorganising work alone could capture the gain without the hours cut is untested.

## Overall

The briefing reaches the right conclusions and states most of them at the right strength. Its errors almost all point the same way: a decline that looks larger than it is, a design trend that looks cleaner than it is, a per-worker loss that looks slightly smaller than it is, and a mechanism that looks better established than it is. None of these changes the bottom line. Fixing them, and adding cost, would make the briefing reliable for the working group.
